what_its_for: Penicillin G is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as strep throat, pneumonia, syphilis, Lyme disease, and infections of the skin, ears, and other parts of the body. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It does NOT work for viral infections like colds or the flu.
how_to_take: Penicillin G is usually given as an injection (shot) by a doctor, nurse, or healthcare provider — either into a muscle (like your buttock or thigh) or directly into a vein through an IV. You will NOT be giving this medication to yourself at home in most cases. If you are prescribed the oral liquid form (Penicillin V is the oral version), take it on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, about 30 minutes before or 2 hours after a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Always finish the full course of treatment, even if you start feeling better early.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on the type and seriousness of your infection, your weight, your age, and your kidney function. Doses can range widely — for example, from a single injection for some infections (like syphilis) to multiple daily injections for serious infections like pneumonia or heart valve infections. For children, the dose is based on body weight. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled injection at a clinic or hospital, contact your healthcare provider right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not double up on doses. If you are taking an oral form and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Injectable Penicillin G should be stored and handled by your healthcare team — do not store it at home unless specifically instructed. If you are given a take-home supply, store it in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it away from light. Do not use it past the expiration date on the label. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other antibiotics, vitamins, or supplements without telling your doctor, as some can interact with Penicillin G. Do not stop your treatment early, even if you feel better — stopping too soon can allow the infection to come back stronger and harder to treat. Avoid alcohol in large amounts during your treatment. Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, especially blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin), other antibiotics, or oral contraceptives (birth control pills), as Penicillin G may reduce their effectiveness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help RIGHT AWAY if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (signs include hives, rash, itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness — this is called anaphylaxis and is a medical emergency); severe diarrhea or diarrhea with blood or mucus (could be a serious bowel infection called C. diff); unusual bruising or bleeding; seizures; confusion or unusual behavior; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; or signs that the infection is getting worse instead of better. Also call if you develop a new rash, fever, or joint pain during treatment.
when_it_works: Many people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. However, it is very important to finish the entire course of antibiotics your doctor prescribed, even if you feel completely better. Stopping too early can allow some bacteria to survive and cause the infection to come back. For some serious infections, full recovery may take several weeks.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Penicillin G is generally considered safe to use during pregnancy and is often the antibiotic of choice for infections in pregnant women, such as syphilis. Always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. BREASTFEEDING: Small amounts of Penicillin G may pass into breast milk. It is generally considered safe during breastfeeding, but tell your doctor so they can monitor your baby for any signs of diarrhea or rash. CHILDREN: Penicillin G can be used in children, including newborns, at doses adjusted for their weight. ELDERLY: Older adults with reduced kidney function may need a lower dose. Your doctor will check your kidney function if needed. KIDNEY PROBLEMS: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or how often you receive the medication.
